items.title: Bright turns on Ocusell integration so agents enter listings once
items.description: Bright MLS has turned on its live integration with Ocusell ’s listing network, allowing brokers and agents who work across multiple MLSs in the Mid-Atlantic to enter and edit listings once and syndicate them into Bright and other participating MLSs without double data entry, the companies announced Tuesday. The operational launch marks the first major product milestone from the joint venture Bright and Ocusell formed in 2025 and introduces OneList , a co-developed listing input platform built on the Ocusell Network that is designed to give brokerages and MLSs a single, connected listing interface nationwide. Under the integration, brokers and agents can create and modify listings in Ocusell, where data is validated against MLS rules, then push that compliance-checked data directly into Bright and other destination MLSs. The system is built to preserve each MLS’s existing rules, data structures and subscriber entitlements while eliminating one of the most common friction points for agents who belong to multiple MLSs. “We entered into this joint venture to remove friction from the daily work of our brokers and agents,” said Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan, who is also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner. “Our role as an MLS is to adapt to how real estate pros operate and to help them succeed. This partnership with Ocusell is a clear example of that.” The launch comes as the Open Real Estate (ORE) initiative is running a national request for proposal search for a vendor that can deliver “input once, distribute everywhere” listing entry across markets. Ocusell says it is already live across 30 MLSs, and with OneList now operating at Bright, one of the nation’s largest MLSs, the company is positioning its network as a scalable solution for multi-MLS entry. For brokers, the integration is aimed at reducing staff time and compliance risk tied to re-keying listing data into separate MLS systems. Agents can enter listing specifics, photos and disclosures once; the platform then auto-validates those fields against each local MLS’s rules while maintaining existing access and display policies. According to Ocusell, its infrastructure can cut listing creation time by up to 75% and prevent more than 85% of compliance errors. On top of cross-market sync, according to the announcement, the forthcoming OneList interface layers in real-time AI-driven compliance and Fair Housing screening, intelligent media management with automated photo tagging and organization, and integrated listing promotion that lets agents launch targeted marketing campaigns from the listing input workflow. “This is a total game changer for agents, brokers, and home buyers and sellers,” said Steve Mapes , executive in charge of growth strategy at Bright MLS. “When agents aren't stuck doing double data entry because they belong to multiple MLSs, they have more time to serve their clients and do what they do best. Technology should make things better, faster and more efficient, and we’re excited to get this up and running.” “Now is the time for MLSs to help shape what comes next for their brokers,” Hayden Rieveschl , the CEO of Ocusell and a 2026 HousingWire Insider , said in a statement. “Bright and Ocusell are demonstrating what’s possible when you listen to brokers and turn their needs into action. As more brokerages operate across markets, MLSs have an opportunity to remove barriers and make doing business easier.” Why this matters for housing professionals The move reflects a broader shift in organized real estate as large regional brokerages, teams and franchises increasingly span multiple MLS territories while regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys scrutinize how listing data is shared and displayed. For brokers and agents, multi-MLS input has historically meant duplicate work, inconsistent data, higher error rates and delays getting listings in front of buyers across markets. A centralized entry layer like OneList, if widely adopted, could streamline operations for multi-market firms, tighten compliance controls and create more standardized listing data for downstream tools, portals and valuation models. For MLS organizations, the Bright-Ocusell rollout is a signal that listing input may increasingly be handled through connected, vendor-operated platforms rather than bespoke MLS-only interfaces, potentially reshaping how MLSs think about technology procurement, interoperability and data licensing. Ocusell said the integration is live now for active Bright MLS brokerages that manage listings across multiple markets, according to the announcement. Bright said rollout timelines and early-access details for the broader OneList platform will be shared in future communications. items.title: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down
items.description: Court Calif. new-build buyers: Prop 37 funds up to 17% down By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published November 04, 2026, 4:26 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Learn how California's newly passed Proposition 37 changes down payment obligations for buyers eying new construction. Supporting Data: A study suggests the measure could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Processing Content California voters may have delivered a reprieve to local real estate players dealing with weak housing demand. Golden State residents Tuesday passed Proposition 37 by a comfortable margin , agreeing to kick off a unique revenue bond that will help homebuyers cover down payments for new builds. The $25 billion bond could support 190,000 new home purchases statewide, according to one analysis. The ballot measure, spearheaded by a Democrat statehouse veteran, passed alongside the blue wave nationwide as voters reacted to factors including rising costs. Californians also passed Prop 1 on Tuesday, which will allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Prop 37, or the California Middle-Class Homeownership and Family Home Construction Act of 2026, will offer eligible home buyers up to 17% of a newly constructed home's purchase price for homes priced below $1.5 million. Borrowers eligible for the second mortgage must be California residents, occupy the home, and earn less than twice of their area's median income. Homeowners also must put at least 3% down on their purchase. An analysis noted another affordability perk as those consumers wouldn't also have to obtain mortgage insurance . The California Association of Realtors, which backed the proposition, didn't respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Mortgage players, including locally-based lenders and trade groups, didn't weigh in on the measure before Tuesday's election. Although California is one of the nation's most expensive states to buy a home, the proposition could nudge buyers stalled in some of the worst housing market conditions this decade. It can also provide slight relief to homebuilders which have seen demand for home loans on new construction fall notably this summer . How the proposition can boost homebuying An analysis by a consulting firm described the typical savings, such as a homebuyer securing a $27,044 down payment versus a $180,290 on the median-priced California home of approximately $901,450. The study, also citing Zillow and U.S. Census Bureau data suggests that every $1 billion of bond capital could support the construction and purchase of around 7,600 new homes across 21 California metropolitan areas. Additionally, every $1 billion of bond investment could leverage an additional $4.9 billion in spending on construction and related activities. Former Speaker of the California Assembly Robert M. Hertzberg championed the proposition in a recent op-ed , citing the state's massive housing affordability challenges. "Proposition 37 offers middle-class Californians a real chance to put down roots, build equity, and stay in the communities they serve," he wrote. Where the opportunity lies in California According to public statistics from the California Department of Housing and Community Development, the biggest homebuilding opportunity lies in Southern California. Of the 40,309 single-family properties permitted last year, 1,636 were in Los Angeles while 1,294 were in Los Angeles County. Builders however are completing more builds across the state. Of the 34,523 homes completed in 2025 per the database, a leading 1,248 properties were finished in Bakersfield last year. That was followed by Roseville and Elk Grove, outside of Sacramento, and Los Angeles. Andrew Martinez Reporter Andrew Martinez joined National Mortgage News in January 2022. items.title: Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress
items.description: Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January. The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed. The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump , who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence." Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs , raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas. "If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula , CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com. Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas , Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend. Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in. What's on the table Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act . That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts . But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level. In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act , with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines. Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move. Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence. The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding." Loading... Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei leaves the U.S. Capitol surrounded by aides and security after meeting with President Donald Trump on Sept. 29. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images What it means locally While data centers affect property taxes , the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open. Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers. "Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far." The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions. Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas. It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says. "That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities." Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus

items.title: AMH Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results
items.description: AMH Reports Third Quarter 2026 Financial and Operating Results November 4, 2026 Download (opens in new window) Raises Full Year 2026 Guidance LAS VEGAS , Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AMH (NYSE: AMH) (the "Company"), a leading large-scale integrated owner, operator and developer of single-family rental homes, today announced its financial and operating results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Highlights Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% year-over-year to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026. Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. Core Funds from Operations ("Core FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.4% year-over-year to $0.50 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026 and Adjusted Funds from Operations ("Adjusted FFO") attributable to common share and unit holders increased 7.6% year-over-year to $0.45 per FFO share and unit for the third quarter of 2026. Core Net Operating Income ("Core NOI") from Same-Home properties increased by 2.5% year-over-year for the third quarter of 2026. Achieved Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0% in the third quarter of 2026, while generating 2.6% blended rate growth driven by lease spreads of 3.3% and 1.0% on renewals and new leases, respectively. October 2026 leasing results remained seasonally strong with Same-Home Average Occupied Days Percentage of 96.0%, rate growth on new leases of 0.1% and rate growth on renewals of 3.3%. Delivered a total of 498 high-quality and energy-efficient newly constructed homes from our AMH Development Program to our wholly-owned portfolio and unconsolidated joint ventures in the third quarter of 2026. Repurchased and retired 2.4 million of our outstanding Class A common shares at a weighted-average price of $31.39 per share and a total price of $75.0 million in the third quarter of 2026. Raised Full Year 2026 Core FFO attributable to common share and unit holders guidance midpoint by $0.02 per share and unit to $1.97, representing anticipated full year growth of 5.3% over prior year. "AMH had another strong quarter with balanced execution across the platform and resilient demand driving an increase to the midpoint of our Core FFO per share guidance by $0.02 to $1.97 – now representing 5.3% year-over-year growth," stated Bryan Smith, AMH's Chief Executive Officer. "Our high-quality homes in great locations, superior resident experience supported by our technology and data platform, and outstanding team continue to differentiate AMH and drive sector-leading growth as we close out 2026 and turn our attention to 2027." Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Net income attributable to common shareholders totaled $82.3 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $99.7 million, or $0.27 per diluted share, for the third quarter of 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower net gains on property sales and lower other income and expense, net, partially offset by increases in rents and other single-family property revenues exceeding increases in total expenses. On a per diluted share basis, the decrease was partially offset by lower share counts as a result of our share repurchase activity. Rents and other single-family property revenues increased 4.1% to $498.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $478.5 million for the third quarter of 2025. Revenue growth was primarily driven by higher rental rates. Core NOI from our total portfolio increased 5.3% to $278.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $264.3 million for the third quarter of 2025. This growth was driven by a 3.6% increase in core revenues resulting primarily from higher rental rates, partially offset by a 0.3% increase in core property operating expenses. For the Company's Same-Home portfolio, core revenues increased 2.3% to $371.1 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $362.8 million for the third quarter of 2025, which was driven by a 2.4% increase in Average Monthly Realized Rent per property, partially offset by a 30 basis point decrease in Average Occupied Days Percentage. Core property operating expenses from Same-Home properties increased 1.8% to $125.2 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $122.9 million for the third quarter of 2025, primarily driven by higher repairs and maintenance ("R&M") and turnover costs, net. As a result, Core NOI from Same-Home properties increased 2.5% to $246.0 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $239.9 million for the third quarter of 2025. Core FFO attributable to common share and unit holders was $205.1 million, or $0.50 per FFO share and unit, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $196.7 million, or $0.47 per FFO share and unit, for the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted FFO attributable to common share and unit holders was $183.4 million, or $0.45 per FFO share and unit, for the third quarter of 2026, compared to $175.5 million, or $0.42 per FFO share and unit, for the third quarter of 2025. These improvements were primarily attributable to growth in Core NOI from our total portfolio. On a per FFO share and unit basis, the increase was further benefited by lower share counts as a result of our share repurchase activity. The increase was primarily due to increases in rents and other single-family property revenues exceeding increases in total expenses, partially offset by lower other income and expense, net. items.title: Safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. 2050
items.description: Safety has a price, and it will be paid. Cotality analyzed the top 10 safest and riskiest places to live in the U.S. and found that the areas or the country that are least vulnerable to natural catastrophes are also where prices are growing the fastest. In all states, the cost of homeownership is no longer calculated by mortgage payments alone. As the risk of natural disasters increases, insuring a home is increasingly determining the final monthly cost of being a homeowner. At the same time, people are paying more to live in regions where natural catastrophes are of less concern. Pennsylvania recorded some of the most pronounced year-over-year home price growth in August 2026. Arizona and the District of Columbia are poised to see the most price growth in the coming year, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. These states will also be some of the safest come 2050. Safest states in the U.S. State Top Associated Peril Average Annual Loss for All Perils Top 3 Safest Washington D.C. Severe convective storm $42 million Pennsylvania Inland flood $3.2 billion Maryland Severe convective storm $900 million *The safest areas in the country are places where peril exposure and the associated loss rates are smallest. Data source: Cotality, 2026 Washington D.C. remains the safest place in the U.S. today and in 25 years. While Pennsylvania and Arizona fall in the rankings, they remain in the top 10. However, even in the least vulnerable areas of the country, average annual losses from natural catastrophes are projected to jump 39% by 2050. That double-digit surge underscores that even in regions long perceived as safe havens, weather risk—and its financial toll— is climbing . See the true cost Climate Risk Analytics - Chronic Perils Home price pressures are even more pronounced in the areas of the country most exposed to natural hazards. By 2050, the top 10 riskiest areas of the country will see average annual losses spike 52%. Insurance costs, and homeowners’ monthly payments, are increasing alongside those losses. Riskiest states in the U.S. State Top Associated Peril Average Annual Loss for All Perils Top 3 Riskiest Louisiana Inland flood $11.4 billion Mississippi Hurricane wind $4.5 billion Florida Hurricane wind $17.5 billion Data source: Cotality, 2026 Florida alone is responsible for $17.5 billion in projected average annual losses, that’s more than the forecast annual losses of $15.2 billion for all 10 of the safest states combined. Rebuilding a home is a financial burden across all points of the industry. Lenders worry about mortgage payments. Insurers face portfolio profitability concerns. Homeowners can enter the classic default hierarchy: depleting emergency savings, maxing out credit cards, and tapping short-term debt before their financial cushion evaporates and they risk default. Mapping portfolios on historical risk boundaries leaves blind spots. Buyers, lenders, and insurers need property-level clarity before the total investment cost can be judged with confidence and they can implement risk mitigation to build long-term resilience. ‍ Explore more Climate Risk Analytics - Chronic Perils Climate resilience & mitigation measures Geospatial mapping
